issues.legal_issue: Market value in a land-acquisition compensation proceeding may be assessed using comparable pre-notification sales where the acquired land has proven development potential and no better comparable evidence is available.
material_facts: The acquired land abutted a road and was adjacent to an inhabited area, with commercial, industrial, and residential development nearby.
Evidence showed the land had potential for commercial, industrial, and residential use.
Three sale deeds relating to transactions before publication of the acquisition notification supported a market value of a little more than the value adopted by the High Court.
The other sale instances relied on by the acquiring side were mutation orders without the corresponding sale deeds, and were not reliable evidence.
The landowners and the acquiring side produced no other comparable sale exemplars.
issues.conclusion: The Court upheld the High Court’s assessment of the land’s market value based on the three pre-notification sale deeds and found no reason to interfere with that assessment as the starting point for determining compensation.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 23 and 24 of the Land Acquisition Act, market value is the price a willing purchaser would pay a willing seller in normal market conditions, having regard to the land’s existing advantages and potential uses, but excluding advantages arising from the acquisition scheme. Potentiality depends on the land’s condition, situation, use or reasonably possible use, proximity to developed areas, and available or prospective amenities. The Court relied on Thakur Kanta Prasad v. State of Bihar, Prithvi Raj Taneja v. State of M.P., Administrator General of West Bengal v. Collector, Varanasi, Periyar v. State of Kerala, Collector Raigarh v. Hari Singh Thakur, Raghubans Narain v. State of U.P., Kaushalya Devi v. L.A.O. Aurangabad, and Suresh Kumar v. T.I. Trust.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_appeal and comparable_pre_notification_sales_exist and acquired_land_has_proven_development_potential and no_better_comparable_evidence_exists

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The matter is an appeal concerning compensation for land acquired compulsorily.
predicates.comparable_pre_notification_sales_exist: Sale transactions for comparable land occurred before the acquisition notification was published.
predicates.acquired_land_has_proven_development_pot: Evidence shows that the acquired land is reasonably capable of development or use for valuable purposes.
predicates.no_better_comparable_evidence_exists: The parties have not produced more reliable comparable sale evidence than the transactions relied on.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns acquired-land compensation and reliable pre-notification sales exist, proven development potential and the absence of better comparable evidence permit the market value to be assessed from those sales.

issues.legal_issue: The deduction from comparable small-plot sale prices when valuing a larger acquisition depends on the acquisition’s purpose and the circumstances of the land, and may be limited where the land is acquired for productive industrial use.
material_facts: The sale exemplars were of small plots, while the acquisition covered a much larger tract.
The acquired land was intended for a sugar factory, rather than a housing colony, government office, or institution.
The land had potential for industrial, commercial, and residential use, and was situated near existing development and amenities.
The Court considered that an industry could generate continuing returns from the acquired land, unlike a development scheme that sells plots after laying them out.
The High Court had reduced the comparable-sale value by one-third; the Supreme Court instead considered a smaller deduction appropriate.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that a limited deduction from the market value indicated by the sale exemplars was appropriate and assessed compensation using a 10% deduction from the High Court’s market-value figure.
issues.legal_principle: Prices of small developed plots cannot ordinarily be applied directly to a large tract without considering land needed for amenities, development expenses, delay in sale, and investment risk; the deduction depends on the facts and is not automatic. Bhagwathula Samanna v. Special Tehsildar & Land Acquisition Officer holds that deduction may be unjustified where the land is already favorably situated and has building potential. Kasturi v. State of Haryana recognizes that surrounding development can reduce the required deduction. Administrator General of West Bengal v. Collector, Varanasi and Chimanlal v. Special Land Acquisition Officer explain the usual development-related factors. Basant Kumar v. Union of India, K. Vasundara Devi v. Revenue Divisional Officer, and H.P. Housing Board v. Bharat S. Negi concerned deductions in different acquisition settings. The Court distinguished land intended for a continuing productive industry from land acquired for a layout or institutional purpose because the industry may earn continuing returns.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_appeal and comparable_sales_are_small_plots and acquisition_is_for_productive_industry and acquired_land_has_development_potential

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The matter is an appeal concerning compensation for land acquired compulsorily.
predicates.comparable_sales_are_small_plots: The sale transactions used as valuation evidence concern plots substantially smaller than the acquired tract.
predicates.acquisition_is_for_productive_industry: The land is acquired for an industrial use expected to produce goods or other continuing economic returns.
predicates.acquired_land_has_development_potential: Evidence shows that the acquired land is reasonably capable of development or valuable use.

issues.definition: When a large tract is acquired for productive industry and its small-plot comparables and development potential are established, the rule calls for only a limited deduction from the comparable-sale value.

issues.legal_issue: Landowners awarded compensation for compulsorily acquired land are entitled to the applicable statutory additions and interest.
material_facts: The landowners sought enhanced compensation for land compulsorily acquired.
The Court revised the compensation assessment and expressly held that the landowners were also entitled to statutory additions and interest.
issues.conclusion: The landowners were entitled to the statutory amount, solatium, and interest provided for by the Land Acquisition Act.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 23(1-A) and 23(2) of the Land Acquisition Act provide for the statutory amount and solatium, respectively, and Section 28 provides for interest. The Court applied those provisions to the compensation awarded for the acquired land.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The matter is an appeal concerning compensation for land acquired compulsorily.
predicates.landowners_are_awarded_compensation_for_: The landowners receive an award of compensation for their acquired land.

issues.definition: When landowners are awarded compensation in an acquired-land compensation appeal, they receive the applicable statutory additions and interest.
